text: Linguistic feedback and episodic memory improve later trials without model-weight updates, as supported by Reflexion (Shinn et al.).
Experience can be consolidated into reusable, portable skills separate from the core prompt, as demonstrated by Voyager (Wang et al.).
Multi-agent peer review improves outcomes, but peer consensus is not a substitute for factual validation.
Multi-agent systems incur substantial token overhead and are only economically justified for parallel, high-value work.
Agent organizations can become more effective yet less aligned than individual agents.
The onboarding compiler that parses job descriptions into skills, permissions, and qualification tests is feasible with acceptable human effort.
Evidence-gated learning with held-out evaluation prevents policy and skill drift.
The HR-shaped organizational lifecycle vocabulary (employment records, promotion, reassignment) adds engineering value beyond standard IAM and config-as-code primitives.
Credential revocation, least-privilege access, and short-lived tokens are sound and necessary governance controls for agentic systems.
Evaluator independence is undermined when the operator and evaluator share the same base model lineage.
A single agent with versioned prompts, trace logging, approval gates, and tool restrictions may capture most of the value of the full organizational OS at lower complexity.
Offboarding is difficult to make complete because derived credentials, delegated work, and memory embedded in shared skills are hard to fully revoke.
Human oversight approval queues will degrade to rubber-stamping under production load, undermining governance value.
Skill libraries may become incoherent at organizational scale due to versioning conflicts, combinatorial interactions, and dead-skill accumulation.
The 90-day prototype should include a multi-agent manager or control bot class to test coordination early.
Prompt injection through tool outputs or retrieved content is a high-severity risk for any tool-using agent with external inputs.
Successful lifecycle drill execution (revocation, rollback, reassignment) should be a hard prerequisite for any go decision, independent of economic results.
The evidence-gated learning pipeline and content-addressed configuration are the strongest novel contributions of the proposed architecture.
Bot identity and learned skills should persist across foundational model upgrades without requiring full re-onboarding.
Risk tier classification for change-control gating is itself an unsolved open problem that the governance matrix presupposes.
